A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GTDL feature-interaction study despite the changed title and framing. The text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, including v2's landscape results table, and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on three MVN and three SCM datasets, including graph-recovery ROC AUC, predictive R2, true-edge pruning, and node-level versus graph-level comparisons.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds TabPFN and XGBoost comparisons, statistical tests, and evaluations with up to 100,000 training samples.

M1.justification: The evaluated GTDL architectures, attention aggregation and normalization, INCE conversion, and true-edge masking procedure remain unchanged. The graph-level T2G-Former adaptation already appears in v1. V2's revised evaluation graph and additional experiments do not establish a new predictive algorithm or model component.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same six synthetic, numerical, ten-feature MVN and SCM datasets for regression and interaction recovery. V2's larger-sample experiment uses two retained SCM datasets; it changes sample sizes and settings, not dataset or task coverage. Real-world and categorical-data evaluations remain future work.

E2.justification: V2 adds TabPFN and XGBoost as evaluated predictive baselines alongside the retained four GTDL methods and BDgraph (Section 3.4, Figure 5, and Table 9). These materially broaden comparison to a pretrained tabular model and boosted trees; in v1 they were discussed or cited but not evaluated.

E3.justification: The main 1,000–4,000-sample protocol remains, but Appendix D.2 adds experiments up to 100,000 samples on SCM 0 and SCM 1 using default rather than tuned hyperparameters. V2 also specifies moralization and marginalization for the SCM evaluation graph, replacing v1's description based on the DAG and discarded roots. This revises the documented reference structure without establishing exactly which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.2 extends the existing sample-size sensitivity analysis to test whether poor graph recovery and diminishing pruning benefits persist with much more data. This is a targeted robustness extension. The node-level versus graph-level ablation is retained from v1's Section 4.2 and Figure 6, moving to v2's Appendix D.3 and Figure 13.

E5.justification: V1 already reports ten runs per fold and displays error bars. V2 identifies the bars as standard deviations and adds linear mixed-effects significance testing, with graph type as a fixed effect and fold as a random effect (Appendix C.1). Figures 5 and 10 and Table 9 report p-values. No increase in the main experiment's run count is stated.

E6.justification: V2 adds baseline results, significance outcomes, and large-sample curves. For example, Table 9 newly reports SCM 0 R2 at 1,000 samples of 0.7199 for TabPFN and 0.6038 for XGBoost. SCM graph-recovery curves also change alongside the revised reference graph, so these are not straightforward same-setting performance gains. The broad pruning and structural-recovery conclusions remain.

T1.justification: V2 formally distinguishes the undirected conditional-independence graph from asymmetric learned weights and specifies their expected symmetric support (Section 2). It also adds the moralization and marginalization construction for SCM ground truth (Section 3.1 and Appendix B). These refine the mathematical target beyond v1's graph description; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims of poor interaction recovery and improved prediction under true-edge pruning remain. V2 adds a stronger mechanism-level conclusion that attention and message passing do not capture interactions as intended, while presenting the contribution as a systematic evaluation framework. V1 emphasizes a broader position advocating trustworthy, interpretable, structure-aware GTDL.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands the discussion of applicability and interpretive limits. Sections 3.1 and 5 acknowledge small synthetic graphs, limited realism, the contested interpretation of attention, and possible information loss from aggregation. Section 4.2 also interprets the new baseline comparisons. These substantive qualifications and explanations were largely absent from v1.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the reported anonymous code-access link with a named GitHub repository, adds XGBoost's hyperparameter space in Table 7, and specifies that TabPFN is not tuned and the large-sample experiments use default hyperparameters. The original GTDL implementation adaptations, main training settings, and search spaces are retained.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning around tabular foundation models, explaining why TabPFN, TabICL, and LimiX are excluded from direct attention-based graph interpretation. It also contrasts its synthetic structures with TabNet and Table2Graph and engages the attention-as-explanation debate. These substantive additions, with new graphical-model and statistical references, go beyond bibliographic restyling.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten from a position-paper narrative into an empirical analysis. The advantages list and call to action are removed, graph interpretation receives expanded explanation, and limitations become explicit. The data-generation and experimental appendices exchange order, and supplementary results gain dedicated subsections.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the explanatory schematics, adds a literature-summary table and SCM graph-conversion diagrams, and redesigns performance plots with baseline comparisons and p-value panels. Tables 8–9 provide numerical counterparts to the plots, and Figures 11–12 display new large-sample results. The retained node-versus-graph figure moves to the appendix, alongside a document-wide journal-format change.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the study's evidential basis: it makes the graph-recovery target explicit, addresses the limited training-size range, contextualizes prediction with strong baselines, and documents uncertainty and fold-aware significance tests. Its new limitations discussion also exposes assumptions left largely implicit in v1. The stronger claim about attention and message-passing mechanisms remains broader than the graph-extraction evidence, but the gains in experimental support and transparency provide a clear substantial net improvement.
